outcomes.text: Explain the global distribution and causes of earthquakes, volcanoes and tsunamis.
Describe plate boundaries from divergent, convergent and conservative movement.
Explain intra-plate earthquakes and hot-spot volcanoes from mantle plumes.
Explain plate tectonics: Earth's structure, convection, subduction, ridge push, slab pull, sea-floor spreading, palaeomagnetism.
Describe how these processes work at destructive, constructive, collision and transform margins.
Explain how physical processes affect eruption type, earthquake magnitude and focal depth (Benioff zone).
Explain how seismic waves cause fracturing, shaking, liquefaction and landslides.
Describe volcanic hazards: lava, pyroclastic flows, ash, gases, lahars and jokulhlaups.
Explain how sub-marine earthquakes at subduction zones cause tsunamis.
Define hazard and disaster, vulnerability, resilience thresholds and the hazard risk equation.
Apply the Pressure and Release (PAR) model to hazards in context.
Assess social and economic impacts of tectonic hazards in developed, emerging and developing countries.
Use the Mercalli, Moment Magnitude and VEI scales to measure magnitude and intensity.
Compare earthquakes, volcanoes and tsunamis through hazard profiles.
Use event profiles to show impact severity in countries at different development levels.
Explain how unequal access to education, housing, healthcare and income affects vulnerability and resilience.
Explain how governance and geography (density, isolation, urbanisation) affect resilience.
Compare contrasting hazard events to show interaction of physical and human factors.

subtopics.title: Trends and patterns in tectonic disasters

outcomes.text: Interpret tectonic disaster trends since 1960 and judge the reliability of the data.
Explain how tectonic mega-disasters have regional or global significance.
Explain multiple-hazard zones and how hydrometeorological hazards add to tectonic disasters.
Explain how accuracy of prediction and forecasting depends on the hazard type and place.
Describe the hazard management cycle: response, recovery, mitigation, preparedness.
Use Park's model to compare hazard responses in areas at different development stages.
Describe strategies to modify the event: zoning, resistant design, defences, lava diversion.
Describe strategies to modify vulnerability: monitoring, prediction, education, preparedness.
Describe strategies to modify loss: aid, insurance, NGOs and community action.
Describe the chronology of glacial and interglacial periods since the Pleistocene.
Explain the causes of climate change: Milankovitch cycles, solar output, atmospheric gases, volcanoes.
Define the cryosphere and classify ice masses by scale and location.
Describe present-day high latitude ice sheets and evidence of Pleistocene extent.
Describe glaciated uplands today and relict landscapes from the Pleistocene.
Describe the distribution of periglacial areas and permafrost with its active layer.
Explain periglacial processes: nivation, frost heave, freeze-thaw, solifluction.
Explain formation of periglacial landforms such as ice wedges, patterned ground, pingos, loess.
Explain mass balance and the equilibrium between accumulation and ablation, with feedback.
Describe accumulation and ablation processes.
Explain variations in accumulation and ablation rates and their effects over time.
Compare movement rates of polar and temperate glaciers.
Explain glacier movement by basal slip, regelation creep and internal deformation.
Explain factors controlling rate of movement, such as altitude, basal temperature, slope and lithology.
Explain how glaciers alter landscapes through erosion, entrainment, transport and deposition.
Describe glacial landforms at macro, meso and micro scale in sub-glacial, marginal, proglacial and periglacial settings.
Explain how landforms create upland and lowland landscapes that show former ice extent.
Explain erosion by abrasion, quarrying, plucking, crushing and basal melting, with freeze-thaw and mass movement.
Explain formation of cirques, arêtes, pyramidal peaks, troughs, hanging valleys and ribbon lakes.
Explain ice-sheet scouring landforms: roches moutonnées, knock and lochan, crag and tail.
Explain formation of moraines and drumlins.
Explain lowland depositional features: till plains, lodgement and ablation till.
Use landform assemblages to reconstruct former ice extent, movement and provenance.
Describe water movement in supraglacial, englacial and sub-glacial flows.
Compare glacial and fluvioglacial deposits by stratification, sorting, imbrication and grading.
Explain formation of kames, eskers, kame terraces, sandurs, proglacial lakes, meltwater channels and kettleholes.
Explain cultural and environmental value of relict and active glaciated landscapes.
Assess economic importance of glaciated landscapes: farming, mining, HEP, tourism, forestry.
Describe unique biodiversity of tundra and the role of these areas in water and carbon cycles.
Describe natural and human threats to glaciated landscapes, such as avalanches, outburst floods, tourism and reservoirs.
Explain how human activity degrades fragile ecology: erosion, trampling, landslides, deforestation.
Explain how climate change alters mass balance and the hydrological cycle, e.g. Himalayan glaciers.
Explain roles of stakeholders and approaches from protection to multiple economic use, e.g. Yosemite.
Explain legislative frameworks that protect and conserve landscapes at varied scales.
Explain how climate change makes management harder and needs coordinated action.
Describe the littoral zone: backshore, nearshore, offshore.
Classify coasts by geology, sea level, rivers, waves and tides.
Compare rocky coasts with coastal plain landscapes (sandy and estuarine).
Explain concordant and discordant coasts from geological structure.
Describe Dalmatian and Haff concordant coasts, and headlands and bays.
Explain how bedding, jointing, dip, faulting and folding affect morphology, erosion and micro-features.
Explain how lithology and unconsolidated material affect rates of recession.
Explain differential erosion producing complex cliff profiles.
Explain how vegetation stabilises dunes and salt marshes through succession.
Compare constructive and destructive waves and their effects on beaches.
Explain erosion processes: hydraulic action, corrosion, abrasion, attrition.
Explain erosional landforms: notches, platforms, cliffs, cave-arch-stack-stump.
Explain sediment transport by wave attack angle, longshore drift, tides and currents.
Explain depositional landforms: beaches, spits, bars, tombolos, cuspate forelands.
Use the sediment cell concept (sources, transfers, sinks) and dynamic equilibrium.
Explain weathering's role in sediment production and recession.
Describe mass movement: blockfall, slumping, landslides.
Describe mass movement landforms: rotational scars, talus slopes, terraced cliffs.
Explain eustatic and isostatic causes of sea level change.
Describe emergent and submergent coastlines, such as raised beaches, rias and fjords.
Assess contemporary sea level risks from warming and tectonics.
Explain causes of rapid recession, including human influences like dredging.
Explain how subaerial processes work together to influence recession.
Explain why recession rates vary with wind, fetch, tides, seasons and storms.
Explain local factors and sea level rise that raise flood risk, e.g. Bangladesh.
Describe storm surges and their short-term impacts.
Assess how climate change may raise flood risk and the uncertainty involved.
Assess economic and social losses from coastal recession.
Assess consequences of flooding and storm surges for coastal communities.
Explain how climate change may create environmental refugees.
Evaluate hard engineering: groynes, sea walls, rip rap, revetments, breakwaters.
Evaluate soft engineering: beach nourishment, cliff re-grading, dune stabilisation.
Explain sustainable management for future threats and the local conflicts it can cause.
Explain littoral cells and ICZM as holistic, sustainable strategies.
Explain Shoreline Management Plans, cost benefit analysis and environmental impact assessment.
Explain conflicts between players and winners and losers, e.g. Happisburgh and Chattogram.
Define globalisation as widening, deepening global connections and flows of goods, capital, information, people.

Describe environmental problems and health effects in developing communities.
Describe social and environmental problems in deindustrialised developed regions.
Explain rural-urban migration and megacity growth with its challenges.
Explain increased international migration to global hubs and its low- and high-wage patterns.
Assess costs and benefits of migration for host and source locations.
Explain cultural diffusion through TNCs, media, tourism and migration and the spread of westernised culture.

Explain opposition to globalisation from some groups and governments.

Compare development and environmental trends between regions since 1970.
Explain social, political and cultural tensions in mixed societies, e.g. rise of nationalism in Europe.

Contrast groups that retain cultural identity with those that embrace change, e.g. First Nations.
Explain local sourcing (Transition towns) as a response to globalisation and its costs and benefits.
Evaluate fair trade and ethical consumption schemes.
Explain recycling's role in managing resource consumption and ecological footprints.
Classify economic activity by sector and employment type.
Link differences in economic activity to health, life expectancy and education.
Link pay inequalities to quality of life indices.
Describe changing functions and demographic characteristics, such as gentrification.
Explain change using physical factors, connectedness, history and planning.
Measure change with employment, demography, land use and deprivation indicators.
Explain how global to regional influences shaped your chosen places.
Show how places can be represented in contrasting ways beyond statistics.
Explain how continuity and change have shaped people's lives in your places.
Describe successful regions such as Silicon Valley and their high property prices and skill shortages.
Explain spirals of decline after economic restructuring, e.g. the Rust Belt.
Explain why perceived need for regeneration varies.
Describe variations in community engagement.
Explain how age, ethnicity, gender, length of residence and deprivation affect attachment to places.
Explain conflicts between groups over regeneration priorities.

Use different media as contrasting evidence.
Explain how representations influence perceived need for regeneration.
Explain infrastructure investment such as high speed rail in regenerating regions.
Explain how planning laws, house building targets and affordability affect regeneration.
Explain how migration and capital market deregulation decisions affect investment.
Explain how local governments compete for investment with plans and science parks.
Explain the role of local interest groups and tensions between preservation and change.
Describe regeneration strategies: retail, tourism, sport, and rural diversification.
Explain rebranding using media to improve place image for investors.
Explain rebranding of deindustrialised UK cities around industrial heritage, e.g. Glasgow.
Describe rural rebranding based on heritage, literary links, farm diversification and outdoor pursuits.
Assess economic success by income, poverty and employment changes compared with other areas.
Assess social progress through reduced inequality, deprivation and better life expectancy.
Judge success by improvements in the living environment.
Study urban regeneration strategies, e.g. Salford Quays, and contested local decisions.
Judge outcomes of urban strategies using economic, social, demographic and environmental variables.
Explain why stakeholders judge urban success by different criteria.
Study rural restructuring strategies, e.g. North Antrim coast, and contested decisions.
Judge outcomes of rural strategies using multiple variables.
Explain why stakeholders judge rural success by different criteria.
Describe uneven UK population growth, e.g. London versus the north-east.
Explain how structure and density vary along the rural-urban continuum.
Explain how fertility, mortality and migration shape population structure.
Describe variation in gender and ethnicity within and between settlements.
Explain levels of cultural diversity through clustering, accessibility, physical factors and planning.
Explain how fertility, mortality and migration change cultural characteristics.

subtopics.title: Connections shaping demographic and cultural character

outcomes.text: Explain how global to regional influences shaped your chosen places.
Show how places can be represented in contrasting ways.
Explain how continuity and change in demography and culture affected people's lives.
Explain how urban places are perceived differently over time, from dangerous Victorian London to attractive today.

Describe the range of rural areas from remote to retirement and commuter villages.

subtopics.title: Evaluating how people view living spaces

outcomes.text: Use statistics to judge positive or negative images of a local place.
Use different media as contrasting evidence of image.
Explain how representations influence perceptions of cultural and demographic issues.

subtopics.title: Diverse culture and society in the UK

outcomes.text: Explain how internal UK movement creates uneven demographic and cultural patterns.
Explain how international migration from former colonies and the EU changed UK culture.

Describe how ethnicity shapes urban areas through shops, worship and leisure, e.g. Southall.
Explain how experiences of living spaces change across generations.

subtopics.title: Managing change in diverse rural places

outcomes.text: Study how groups view a rural living space and strategies, e.g. Lake District National Park Partnership.

Explain why stakeholders judge rural success differently.

units.title: Area of study 3: Physical Systems and Sustainability

topics.title: Topic 5: The Water Cycle and Water Insecurity

outcomes.text: Explain the global water cycle as a closed system driven by solar and gravitational energy.
Compare sizes of water stores and annual fluxes.
Explain the water budget limit, residence times and non-renewable stores.
Describe drainage basin inputs, flows and outputs.
Explain how climate, soils, vegetation, geology and relief affect the system.
Explain how humans disrupt the cycle through deforestation, land use, reservoirs and abstraction.
Explain water budgets and how climate type influences them.
Explain river regimes using contrasting basins such as Yukon, Amazon and Indus.
Explain storm hydrograph shapes from physical and human factors.
Explain meteorological and hydrological drought, longer trends and ENSO cycles.
Explain how over-abstraction increases drought risk.
Explain drought impacts on ecosystems and their resilience.
Explain meteorological causes of flooding: storms, prolonged rain, monsoon, snowmelt.
Explain how land use change and hard engineering worsen flood risk.
Assess environmental and socio-economic flood damage, e.g. UK floods 2007 or 2012.

subtopics.title: Climate change and the water cycle

outcomes.text: Explain how climate change affects precipitation and evaporation.
Explain effects on snow and glacier mass, reservoirs, permafrost, soil moisture and runoff.
Explain how ENSO and global warming increase uncertainty over water security.
Describe water stress and scarcity thresholds and the global pattern.
Explain physical and human causes of water insecurity.
Explain how rising demand pressures the finite water resource.
Explain physical and economic scarcity and why water prices vary.
Explain water's importance for development and wellbeing, and problems of inadequate supply.

Evaluate sustainable schemes: restoration, conservation, smart irrigation, recycling, e.g. Singapore.
Explain integrated basin management and water-sharing treaties.

Explain ocean carbon sequestration by phytoplankton, the carbonate pump and thermohaline circulation.
Explain terrestrial photosynthesis and respiration.
Explain storage as soil organic matter and decomposition.
Explain how atmospheric carbon controls the greenhouse effect, temperature and precipitation.
Explain how photosynthesis regulates the atmosphere and stored carbon supports soil health.
Explain how fossil fuel combustion changed carbon pathways and stores.
Describe energy consumption and mix: primary and secondary, renewable and non-renewable.
Explain how energy access depends on availability, cost, technology, perception and development, e.g. USA versus France.
Explain the roles of TNCs, OPEC, consumers and governments in energy supply.
Explain the mismatch between fossil fuel supply and demand regions.
Explain energy pathways and their disruption, e.g. Russian gas to Europe.

Evaluate renewable and nuclear energy and their contribution to energy security.

Evaluate radical technologies such as carbon capture, hydrogen fuel cells and electric vehicles.
